## Research loop this week
* Checkpoint 1 (2026-10-27): Leverage should follow the expected premium (Kelly: f = premium / variance). Try valuation-scaled leverage; widen leverage grids; lever the bond sleeve alone.
* Checkpoint 2 (2026-10-27): Map the expected-value frontier so the leverage choice is explicit. Rank only strategies an ordinary margin account can hold (<=2x) separately from futures-only ones.
* Checkpoint 3 (2026-10-27): Start forward paper accounts (deployable champion, research champion 60/40+SMA10 x3, 60/40 benchmark). Next: alternative trend signals under leverage, financing via leveraged ETFs (daily-reset decay), regime-specific leverage caps.
* Checkpoint 4 (2026-10-27): Champion unchanged. Seasonality goes on a watch list, not into the portfolio. Next: model leveraged-ETF daily-reset costs exactly with daily data, lifecycle de-leveraging, and combining the valuation and trend signals in one leverage rule.
* Checkpoint 5 (2026-10-27): New champion: recovery leverage (2x/3x via SSO/UPRO-style ETFs, cash otherwise). Added a 'deployable via ETFs' flag. Opened a forward paper account for it; the old 2x account continues as the margin champion. Next: when to exit faster in crashes (daily signal with a band), and a stock/bond version of recovery leverage.
* Checkpoint 6 (2026-10-27): New champion by the loop rule (beats on test and forward median): recovery+ = 2x S&P (3x after >15% falls) while the S&P is above its 10-month average OR up over 12 months; 2x 7-10y Treasuries (UST) otherwise. The previous champion keeps its paper account for comparison. Watch item: stock-bond correlation regimes (2022, 1970s) are this rule's weak spot. Next: a bond-trend gate on the off-asset (hold bonds only when bonds are above their own 10-month average), then lifecycle de-leveraging.
* Checkpoint 7 (2026-10-27): New champion: equal-weight ensemble (3x trend + valuation + recovery+), no fitted weights. New champion rule: rank by WORST era across 1880-1929, 1930-1956, 1957-1990 and 1991-2026; a challenger must not lose to the incumbent in any era (research.beats_everywhere); round-number, literature parameters only; the walk-forward selection return is reported as the honest estimate of what the loop itself can deliver. The only truly unseen data is the forward paper record from 2026-09. Data gap: the valuation sleeve needs monthly S&P earnings after 2023-06 (currently frozen at the last value).
* Checkpoint 8 (2026-10-27): Champion unchanged (ensemble: 3x trend + valuation + recovery+, worst era 13.1%). Both ideas go to the explored list. Multi-horizon trend may still work across MANY markets (its published setting), which needs more data. Next: (1) diversify the trend sleeve across markets once data is reachable (FRED has gold, oil, dollar index and international indices); (2) a daily crash exit for the trend sleeve, tested on FRED daily S&P 2016-2026 plus the DJIA 2007-2016 file; (3) lifecycle / fixed-fraction de-leveraging.
* Checkpoint 9 (2026-10-27): No champion change. One daily era can't pass the worst-era rule, and daily data before 2007 is not available offline. The banded daily 200-day rule (3x) joins the real-time simulation as a NEW account, checked every trading day (live_sim gained a daily mode). If it keeps up in real time AND long daily history becomes available, test it as the ensemble's trend sleeve. Next: multi-market trend data (FRED NIKKEI225 since 1949, trade-weighted dollar, oil) and lifecycle de-leveraging.
* Checkpoint 10 (2026-10-28): Champion unchanged under the current rule (US worst era). The trade-off (about 1.4 points a year of worst-era growth and lower expected wealth, for far better survival in a Japan-style market) is a risk-appetite choice for the owner, reported to them. The lower-leverage ensemble joins the real-time simulation as a NEW account. Protocol addition: champion candidates now also report a Japan stress test (Exp 19) for their testable sleeves. Next: international markets on FRED for more out-of-sample tests; a valuation proxy for Japan (dividend yield) if data can be found.
* Checkpoint 11 (2026-10-28): Champion unchanged. On expected growth (the owner's objective) the 3x structure wins out of sample too (median 11.2% vs 9.7%), and it never hit ruin as a 3-sleeve ensemble. The 12-market test is added to the protocol: candidates report median growth, worst-country growth and worst drawdown across the 12 markets; a candidate that goes to zero in any market is excluded. The leverage question (champion vs lower-leverage ensemble) stays with the owner; both run in the real-time simulation.
* Checkpoint 12 (2026-10-28): No champion change: the global sleeve loses 1991-2026 (fails beats_everywhere) and cannot be tested before 1960. It is also harder to implement: 3x on 12 foreign markets needs futures or margin, since there are no daily-reset 3x ETFs for most countries. Kept as evidence that trend plus leverage is not a US-only artefact: diversified across 13 markets it earns more, with shallower falls, over 1961-2026. Next: a deployable 2x global sleeve via country ETFs on margin; ETF data needs a source.
* Checkpoint 13 (2026-10-28): Champion unchanged. Data fix committed. The real-time simulation picks up the corrected valuation signal at its next rebalance (2026-11-02); its past is untouched. Lesson for the loop: check every input series for staleness (last real change), not just the price.
* Checkpoint 14 (2026-10-28): Champion unchanged: for the owner's objective (highest expected long-run growth, no ruin) the champion's leverage is supported out of sample. Its expected growth in an unseen market is the highest tested (about 12%/yr on log terms), with no ruin in 13 markets. If the owner prefers protection against the worst case, about 0.83x of the champion maximises worst-market growth (8.1%), at -78% worst drawdown instead of -85%. Leverage beyond the champion is not tested: the trend sleeve above 3x cannot be held with ETFs.
* Checkpoint 15 (2026-10-28): No champion change. There is no data before 1960, so the worst-era rule cannot be applied; the post-publication edge is small (+0.7 points a year); and implementation needs about 12 country ETFs plus leverage via margin. Recorded as the strongest non-US idea so far; if a deployable global sleeve is built (open direction), use momentum-ranked markets rather than equal weight. The OECD indices are monthly averages, which can flatter momentum. The 12-1 skip and one-month execution lag guard against this, but month-end data would be needed to confirm.
* Checkpoint 16 (2026-10-29): Champion unchanged: neither passes beats_everywhere. Equal weight remains the best way to combine the sleeves, consistent with DeMiguel, Garlappi & Uppal (2009): 1/N is hard to beat out of sample.
* Checkpoint 17 (2026-10-29): No champion change. Model-risk statement for the owner: about two-thirds of the champion's excess over the S&P comes from leverage and one-third from timing (trend + recovery). If markets stopped trending, the champion would still beat the S&P most of the time (84%), but would lag plain leverage. Watch item for the real-time simulation: the trend sleeve's whipsaw costs are the first sign of a no-trend regime. Next: a whipsaw monitor in the weekly report (count of trend-signal flips in the past 12 months vs the historical norm).
* Checkpoint 18 (2026-10-29): No strategy change. The monitor is an early-warning input for the weekly learning review, not a trading rule. Acting on it would be a new strategy and would have to pass the worst-era rule like any other.
* Checkpoint 19 (2026-10-29): Reporting change, no strategy change. The dashboard's 5-year table now shows tax paid and after-tax results. The actual rate depends on the owner's country and account type (a tax-deferred account would remove the drag). Taxes favour buy-and-hold structures; a future candidate could cut realized gains by rebalancing less often (e.g. a ±10% band instead of monthly).
* Checkpoint 20 (2026-10-29): Signals unchanged. Implementation recommendation for a taxable account: trade only beyond a 10% band. A NEW real-time account runs the champion with a 10% band (existing accounts untouched; live_sim gained a band parameter). Important for the owner: in a taxable account the long-run edge over the S&P is about 2 points a year, not 4+. A tax-deferred account keeps the full edge.
* Checkpoint 21 (2026-10-29): Rejected by beats_everywhere (loses 2 of 4 eras). Champion unchanged, worst era 13.1%. Shown to the owner as an example of the worst-era rule catching an overfit-looking improvement.

Champion: ensemble: trend + value + recovery {"trend": 3.0}. Real-time results this short are mostly noise: a strategy's long-run edge shows only over many months; the weekly check looks for behaviour that contradicts the model (e.g. a 3x account not moving about 3x the S&P).

## Lessons this week
* **Behaviour check passed.** Each account's week move matched its stock exposure: 3.0× for the 3× accounts, 2.4× for 60/40 at 4×, 2.1× for the champion (2.09× stocks), and so on down to 0.6× for 60/40. The simulator's leverage, financing and fee model behaves as specified.
* **The ranking is just exposure.** In a rising week, more stock exposure means a higher rank. Nothing here says anything yet about which strategy is better; that needs months, including falling markets.
* **Data:** FRED's S&P 500 series lags its Dow Jones series by two trading days (29–30 Oct missing). If it is still missing on Monday, the November rebalance will use the 28 October close as October's month-end. That cannot flip any signal now: the S&P is about 7% above its 10-month average.
* **Whipsaw monitor:** normal (2 flips in 12 months; the warning level is above 3).
* **Next for the loop:** a fallback for a lagging S&P series (scale the latest Dow Jones move onto the S&P until FRED catches up), and a valuation proxy for the non-US markets of Exp 20–22.
